key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, with liquidity-constrained cardholders driving the null result.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with six-month follow-up (NBER working paper).
why_it_matters: Directly tests the enrollment-vs-real-outcome distinction in a consumer financial product: behavior changed but the substantive outcome did not, exactly the 'vanity enrollment' concern our support team raised.
limitations: credit card debt paydown differs from savings accumulation
the nudge shrouds an option rather than testing opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing directly
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-financial nudge study separating nominal enrollment change from actual behavioral/financial outcome, the core trade-off in the brief.

key_finding: Abstract-only overview summarizing effects of automatic enrollment, default investment options, and framing on DC plan participant behavior, including potential negative effects on engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides broad synthesis of the analogous employer-plan default literature but stays at the level of general survey rather than a specific estimate we can act on.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not consumer fintech
abstract lacks quantitative effect sizes
relevance_reason: General background review of the closest large literature (employer retirement defaults), useful context but replaceable by more specific studies.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity, low contribution rates, and account churn, recommending auto-escalation and re-enrollment reminders as mitigations.
methodology: Narrative/policy discussion paper, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Articulates precisely the disengagement risk our support team raised, but framed for US retirement policy rather than a consumer savings app.
limitations: US employer-mediated retirement plan focus
no primary data or effect sizes given
relevance_reason: States the passive-enrollment disengagement concern central to our internal debate, though in a different regulatory and product setting.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework showing that downstream default effects depend on the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience, and identifies gaps and inconsistencies in prior findings.
methodology: Conceptual review and taxonomy synthesizing the consumer default-effect literature, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict when and why a default's effect on enrollment will or will not persist into engagement and saved amounts — directly informs what to measure over 6-12 months.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical rather than a new empirical estimate
abstract-only, no effect sizes
relevance_reason: The synthesis/review the brief calls for on downstream persistence of default effects, applicable across consumer product settings including ours.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when staying costs substantial drug consumption losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options among Medicare Part D beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows self-directed defaults (no employer intermediary) persist and can actively harm passive low-income users who don't reassess a bad default — direct evidence for the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question and for testing whether the employer-trust mechanism is necessary.
limitations: health-insurance domain, not banking/savings
low-income Medicare population differs from general banking-app users
abstract gives no percentage effect sizes
relevance_reason: Closest analogue to a self-directed (non-employer) default showing persistence and distributional harm, the exact mechanism gap the brief flags.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and of default contribution auto-escalation; steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults hold at the first escalation date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, withdrawal-on-separation, and auto-escalation opt-out. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: enrollment lift is real at signup but shrinks sharply once attrition, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for — a direct check on the 'defaults reliably lift real saving' premise.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives limited breakdown by demographic subgroup
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise real saving, using quantified effect sizes over the medium-to-long run, exactly what the brief asks to weigh against the 'default everyone in' argument.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out, with the default effect stronger when incentives are high and knowledge of enrollment status is low.
methodology: Natural experiment on nationwide auto-enrollment policy using linked administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Provides a clean effect-size estimate of an opt-out default absent an employer intermediary and shows the effect is conditional on incentive salience and consumer knowledge — directly informs how large our own enrollment lift might be and for which users.
limitations: public pension context, not a discretionary consumer savings app
concerns a specifically low-income population
relevance_reason: Quantified default effect and heterogeneity evidence in a government (non-employer) default setting, the closest test of whether the 'trusted intermediary' mechanism is necessary.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions attenuates from 12 months to 36 months, with modest average savings gains at the longer horizon but a significant reduction in savings inequality; a life-cycle model implies a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel, plus a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, quantified answer to whether default effects persist at 12-36 months — showing attenuation — directly bearing on whether an opt-out design's enrollment lift will still show up in actual saved amounts a year later.
limitations: employer/national retirement plans, not a discretionary liquid consumer product
switching-cost estimate is model-based rather than directly observed
relevance_reason: The clearest quantitative evidence on default-effect persistence over exactly the 12+ month horizon the brief asks about.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the advice received compared to no default, especially when the client refused the default.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the helpful-versus-manipulative trade-off in an EU financial-advice context: even an effective default carries a perceived-honesty cost, bearing on both the entry design and how a preset multiplier should be framed to avoid a dark-pattern read.
limitations: wealth-management investment-risk context rather than round-up savings specifically
outcome measured via advice ratings, not actual retention or saved amounts
relevance_reason: Best available EU evidence on when a financial default is perceived as manipulative, directly addressing the brief's reputational-risk criterion.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted (and half still did after three years) the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, largely offsetting aggregate wealth gains from higher participation.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms, a classic auto-enrollment study.
why_it_matters: Establishes the classic anchoring-on-default-level result underlying our concern that a preset round-up multiplier could anchor users at a low rate, but from a now-dated employer-pension context the brief flags as superseded.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401k setting
no publication year given; predates mobile/fintech and current EU regulatory climate
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default finding that later contradicting work in this set (e.g., 'Smaller than We Thought') revisits and updates.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tips finds that 84% of default adherence arises from the combined interaction of deviation costs and opt-out costs, and that adding a lower default tip option captured 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural model estimated on administrative tipping data plus a stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Shows a general mechanism (switching effort plus preference mismatch) behind default adherence and demonstrates that adding one more preset option can capture most of the welfare gain — an analogous consideration for choosing among 1x/2x/5x multiplier presets.
limitations: tipping decisions, not financial savings
no data on long-term retention or enrollment persistence
relevance_reason: Offers a rigorous mechanism-level analysis of default adherence and preset-menu design in a consumer (non-employer) setting, analogous to our multiplier-level decision.

key_finding: Opt-in enrollment in an employer payroll-deduction liquid, withdraw-anytime savings account produced very low take-up (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees), but among those who enrolled, 96% still had a balance and 87% still received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a short-term savings choice-architecture program introduced at five U.K. firms, observed over a 12-month window for enrolled users.
why_it_matters: The closest existing evidence for a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings product: opt-in yields very low nominal enrollment but the enrolled minority is highly persistent, directly informing the trade-off between opt-in's small-but-engaged cohort and opt-out's larger-but-possibly-disengaged one.
limitations: employer payroll channel rather than a standalone consumer app
UK setting; no data on withdrawal amounts or complaint rates
relevance_reason: Nearest available liquid-savings analogue to the round-up product, directly informing the opt-in enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off central to the Entry decision.

key_finding: Under general conditions, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal when the designer and choosers agree on the activity's value; the framework extends to externalities, Pigouvian fees, and cases of normative disagreement between designer and chooser.
methodology: Theoretical/analytical model of optimal default design validated by numerical simulation, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative lens for judging when an opt-out default is actually welfare-optimal versus when disagreement between firm and user interests should push toward opt-in or active choice — useful framing but not tied to our specific product context.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical application to consumer savings
abstract gives no concrete parameter estimates for our setting
relevance_reason: Provides a general economic framework for judging when opt-out defaults are normatively justified versus manipulative, relevant to the distributional/manipulation criterion.

key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns and proposes a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations for assessing when choice-architecture practices like pre-selected defaults cross into manipulation.
methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only, no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out enrollment default or pre-set multiplier would be read as manipulative rather than helpful, directly bearing on the reputational-risk constraint named in the brief.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, no empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly addresses when a default reads as a dark pattern under EU law, the reputational risk named in the brief.

key_finding: At a high 12% default contribution rate, only 25% of employees remained at the default after 12 months (versus roughly half at lower defaults elsewhere), and those who stayed had incomes about a third lower than predicted, showing the default anchored many below their likely preferred rate.
methodology: Administrative data from a single employer plan with a 12% default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Shows that the preset level itself, not just the presence of a default, changes both opt-out behavior and the anchored contribution amount, evidence relevant to choosing the round-up multiplier's preset value.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
no comparison to opt-in or active-choice designs
relevance_reason: Strongest available evidence that a preset level anchors the amount people end up at, even though drawn from a retirement plan setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted ('Trant'), so no substantive finding can be extracted.
methodology: abstract-only; title suggests field experiments on automating payroll savings in the UK, but content is unavailable.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant (payroll savings automation, UK) but the abstract gives no usable evidence to inform either design decision.
limitations: abstract is unreadable/corrupted
payroll-mediated setting, not a standalone consumer app
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to automated savings enrollment, but no usable content is available to verify.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of potential savings.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments across major UK banks on automatic enrollment into an alert feature.
why_it_matters: This is the closest real precedent to our product: a UK bank auto-enrolling customers into a financial-behavior-nudging app feature with measured, economically meaningful effect sizes, directly benchmarking what auto-enrolling users into round-up savings could plausibly achieve.
limitations: alerts, not savings contributions, are the enrolled feature
no multi-year persistence or withdrawal data reported
relevance_reason: Closest prior work: UK consumer banking app feature with automatic enrollment and measured financial outcomes.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into UK pensions raised savings by £32-38/month but this was partially offset by higher unsecured debt (£7/month) and larger mortgage balances (£118), though credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment using randomized roll-out of pension auto-enrollment across ~160,000 UK employers, 41-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Challenges the assumption that default-driven 'savings' are pure gains, since some of the money appears financed by increased borrowing elsewhere, a risk worth measuring if round-up savings similarly reduces available liquidity.
limitations: employer-mediated pension scheme, not a liquid consumer savings app
debt-offset mechanism may not generalize to small liquid round-up sums
relevance_reason: Longest-horizon evidence that default-driven savings gains can be partly illusory once offsetting debt is counted, informing the amount-saved question.

key_finding: Adding a minor 'ordeal' step to health-insurance auto-enrollment cut enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal of an auto-enrollment policy for health insurance, plus a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that moving away from a default toward opt-in can produce large, distributionally uneven drop-offs, directly bearing on who is helped or hurt by our entry design choice.
limitations: health-insurance selection market with adverse-selection dynamics not present in a savings product
no persistence or amount-saved data
relevance_reason: Strong distributional evidence on who a default versus an added enrollment step disproportionately excludes.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign sites raised donations by over $43 million while also raising refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller and less experienced donors.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the timing of default rollout across multiple 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
why_it_matters: The best available real-world causal estimate of a default on a recurring financial commitment, including a direct complaint/backfire proxy (refund requests) and evidence the effect falls hardest on inexperienced, small-money users, precisely the disengagement/complaint risk our support team raised.
limitations: political donations rather than a savings product
no direct measure of long-term retention or withdrawal
relevance_reason: Closest available evidence that pre-checked defaults on recurring monetary commitments increase both uptake and complaint-like backlash, disproportionately among smaller/inexperienced users.

key_finding: A reference-dependent search model and lab experiments show a default raises reservation utility (better choices for defaulters) while those who actively search self-select into finding superior options.
methodology: Theoretical model plus lab experiments on search behavior with a default option; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general mechanism (reference effects, self-selection into active choice) but is too abstract and far from a financial-app setting to directly guide the entry or level decision.
limitations: general lab search task, not a financial or consumer product setting
no enrollment or savings outcome measured
relevance_reason: General behavioral mechanism for why defaults and active search differ; background only.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still present 15 months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the EU DMA choice-screen mandate rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The strongest evidence available that a mandated active-choice screen produces large, durable behavior change away from a default in a mobile app under EU regulation, directly informing whether active choice at onboarding could substitute for opt-out without the disengagement risk.
limitations: browser default choice rather than a savings/financial decision
no direct measure of amount saved or engagement depth
relevance_reason: Best EU-regulatory precedent for active choice screens producing large, persistent shifts away from defaults in a mobile-app context, directly informing the active-choice option in the entry decision.

key_finding: A usability study of nine opt-out privacy choice designs found that 'generalizable' active-choice schemes make opting out far less disruptive (98% not disrupted vs. baseline, a 40-point improvement) at only a slight cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Browser-extension usability study with 410 participants testing nine GPC-based opt-out interface designs.
why_it_matters: Shows a concrete design pattern for making active/opt-out choices low-friction rather than disruptive, useful for designing an active-choice onboarding step that doesn't feel like a dark pattern.
limitations: privacy opt-out setting, not financial enrollment
measures perceived disruption, not actual financial behavior
relevance_reason: Demonstrates a usable, non-disruptive active-choice interface pattern relevant to designing our onboarding active-choice step.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-ups, but for effortful outcomes (actual completion/passing) the default only helped when it carried stronger endorsement and only for students already responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed increased sign-up but no gain in actual outcomes.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up to opt-out for a single exam versus many exams, tracking downstream effortful task completion.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the support team's core worry in a rigorous design: default-driven sign-up can be pure vanity enrollment unless the target outcome and the targeted population are right, and it identifies which subgroup actually benefits.
limitations: university exam context, not a financial product
effort/outcome measure is exam passing, not money saved
relevance_reason: The clearest field-experimental test of whether opt-out defaults produce real effortful engagement or just nominal sign-up, with heterogeneity by responsiveness, the exact 'vanity enrollment' question the brief raises.

key_finding: After target date funds became the default retirement-plan investment option, younger workers' stock allocations rose and older workers' fell in line with the glidepath, but contribution rates barely changed.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's default rule change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly steer an allocation/level choice while leaving an adjacent decision (contribution rate) almost untouched, a useful caution that presetting the round-up multiplier may not spill over into changing whether people opt in at all.
limitations: retirement account asset allocation, not contribution or savings-app enrollment
no consumer fintech setting
relevance_reason: Illustrates that a default can shape one choice dimension strongly while barely moving an adjacent one, a relevant analogy for level-preset spillover concerns.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on Chinese voluntary pension saving, all tested nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative framing and default options, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment': here the default option backfired and reduced willingness to contribute, with heterogeneous effects by demographic group, exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked us to surface.
limitations: hypothetical survey-based willingness rather than real enrollment behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not generalize to an EU banking app
small sample (n=220)
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in this set: a controlled trial where the default-option nudge backfired rather than helped, directly countering the brief's stated internal assumption.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approve of financial nudges (except when framed as manipulation), with strong preference for deliberate 'System 2' interventions and savings-framed messaging over spending-framed ones; transparency did not significantly change ratings.
methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey experiment, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, representative Australian sample, six dependent variables including approval and manipulation.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the reputational/dark-pattern risk of the entry decision: it suggests savings-framed, deliberate ('System 2'-style, i.e. active-choice-like) interventions are rated more favorably than passive ones, and shows transparency alone doesn't drive acceptance — bearing on how opt-out vs active choice will be perceived by users and regulators.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not an actual enrollment decision
measures attitudes/approval, not enrollment or savings behavior
Australian sample, not EU
relevance_reason: Only paper in the set that directly measures perceived manipulativeness and approval of financial nudges, which is exactly the reputational risk axis the brief flags for the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Offering conditional-cash-transfer recipients a bank account instead of cash had no significant average effect on savings, but increased balances for those with previously nonpositive balances.
methodology: Field experiment among CCT beneficiaries comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery of subsidies.
why_it_matters: Weak analogy: shows account access itself (not defaults) can help low-savers, but the setting (aid transfers, not app-based enrollment defaults) is far from the brief's decision.
limitations: studies delivery channel, not enrollment defaults
CCT/aid population, not a consumer banking app user base
no engagement or persistence data beyond balances
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence on savings account access effects, not on default/opt-out enrollment design.

key_finding: Compares automatic-IRA designs with and without an emergency-savings/liquid component, noting contribution amounts and interest access differ by liquidity treatment.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be a program-comparison study of an automatic IRA with an emergency-savings feature.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant to liquid-savings design (round-up pot is liquid), but the abstract fragment gives no usable effect sizes or design detail.
limitations: abstract is a truncated fragment with almost no substantive content
employer/government auto-IRA context, not a consumer banking app
no clear enrollment or persistence data available
relevance_reason: Nominally on-topic (liquid vs. locked automatic savings) but abstract provides too little information to be actionable.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most auto-enrolled employees stuck to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation ('default' behavior) even years later.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment at one large U.S. corporation comparing 401(k) elections pre- and post-automatic-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: The original demonstration that defaults both raise sign-ups and anchor the chosen contribution level — the direct precedent for our concern that a preset round-up multiplier will anchor users rather than reflect their true preference.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
locked, illiquid savings unlike round-up pots
single-firm case study
relevance_reason: Foundational paper establishing the anchoring-on-default mechanism the brief's Level decision is worried about, but off-domain (employer 401k).

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatically-enrolled and voluntarily-enrolled defined-contribution retirement plan participants.
methodology: abstract-only; unknown design.
why_it_matters: Could bear on default-vs-voluntary enrollment differences, but with no abstract there is nothing to weigh against existing stronger evidence.
limitations: no abstract provided
employer retirement plan setting, not consumer app
recency (2026) unverified with no content
relevance_reason: Topically adjacent but unusable without an abstract.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority status predict both under-saving and early withdrawal from pension accounts around an Estonian reform allowing early withdrawal, creating 'double jeopardy' for already under-saved groups.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension early-withdrawal policy reform.
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the support team's worry that passively-enrolled, disengaged users will withdraw money early, and shows this risk concentrates among low-trust and minority groups — relevant to distributional harm analysis.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a self-directed consumer savings feature
correlational survey data, no experimental default manipulation
Estonian institutional context may not generalize to EU app users broadly
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on who is likely to disengage/withdraw, echoing the brief's concern about which users a default enrollment would harm.

key_finding: In a 24,303-person G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccination policy reduced stated intentions to comply and reduced approval of the policy, revealing backlash risk from transparency about defaults.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a default-enrollment nudge.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that making a default salient/transparent can backfire and generate disapproval — a caution against assuming an opt-out default is either invisible or automatically accepted, relevant to the manipulation/dark-pattern risk the brief flags.
limitations: vaccination policy setting, not financial products
hypothetical policy, not actual enrollment behavior
measures stated intentions, not real savings enrollment
relevance_reason: Contradicts the implicit premise that defaults are costlessly accepted once disclosed, bearing on reputational risk of an opt-out design.

key_finding: Survey analysis finds automatic enrollment and employer matching are associated with higher retirement-plan participation among U.S. Millennials.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Adds another correlational confirmation that auto-enrollment raises participation, but offers nothing new beyond stronger causal evidence already in the set.
limitations: employer retirement plan context
correlational, not causal
no persistence, amount-saved, or anchoring data
relevance_reason: Redundant confirmatory evidence on default-driven participation in an employer setting, weaker than causal studies already available.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, each $1 of subsidy spending (requiring active choice) raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic/passive employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation; ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic contributions, while the wealthier, more sophisticated 15% 'active savers' mainly shift assets across accounts.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish savings accounts, comparing active-choice tax subsidies to passive/automatic employer contributions.
why_it_matters: The strongest available causal evidence that automatic/default mechanisms move actual saved amounts (not just nominal enrollment) far more than active-choice mechanisms, and that the people helped by defaults are exactly the less sophisticated, passive majority — directly bears on whether enrollment lift is 'vanity' and on who benefits from an opt-out design versus active choice.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts, not liquid consumer savings
Denmark's institutional context (mandatory pension infrastructure) differs from an EU consumer banking app
measures subsidy-induced shifting versus automatic contribution, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment design per se
relevance_reason: Provides the clearest large-sample evidence that passive/default mechanisms move real saved amounts and disproportionately help less-sophisticated users, the exact distributional trade-off the brief asks about, even though the setting is retirement accounts.

key_finding: Proposes and tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option — as a more effective alternative or complement to automatic enrollment when opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught, across two field experiments.
methodology: Literature review plus two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against standard opt-in/opt-out framing.
why_it_matters: This is the closest prior work specifically comparing active-choice designs to defaults, directly informing the Entry decision: whether active choice can capture most of the enrollment benefit of opt-out without its disengagement/manipulation costs, and how to design the active-choice screen itself.
limitations: field experiments include health/medication-adherence settings, not financial products
no direct measurement of downstream savings amount or 6-12 month persistence
older (2011) work, though conceptually still the reference point for active choice
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and tests the active-choice mechanism the brief is deciding between, including a refined variant ('enhanced active choice') relevant to onboarding screen design.

key_finding: Synthesizes the behavioral household-finance literature, covering consumption/savings, product design, choice architecture, and disclosure interventions across consumer financial contexts, not solely employer retirement plans.
methodology: Narrative review/chapter summarizing empirical regularities and behavioral interventions in household finance.
why_it_matters: Serves as the review-level synthesis of default and choice-architecture effects in consumer (not just employer) financial settings, giving a broader evidence base and caveats for weighing the enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off than any single study.
limitations: broad narrative overview rather than a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers many topics beyond enrollment defaults, diluting specificity
abstract-only detail on any single finding
relevance_reason: Provides the review/synthesis-level evidence the brief explicitly asks for, framed around consumer (not only employer) financial behavior.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of enrollees initially accepted the default 2-3% contribution rate and default conservative fund, with half still at the default rate/fund after three years, offsetting higher participation against lower per-person savings.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The clearest longitudinal demonstration that a preset default level anchors contribution rates for years and can offset participation gains — the precedent the brief's Level decision (preset multiplier vs blank field) should be measured against.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, illiquid retirement savings, not a consumer app
no active-choice comparison arm
pre-2010s data from an era with different digital/behavioral norms
relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative evidence on default-level anchoring and its persistence over years, directly analogous to the round-up-multiplier anchoring question.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to default-enrolled versus opt-in salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% matching incentive), an effect the authors attribute mainly to present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios rather than employer endorsement, and default assignment also increased later active decisions to save.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with multiple treatment arms isolating mechanisms behind the default effect (present bias vs. cognitive cost vs. endorsement).
why_it_matters: Directly tests why defaults work and finds the effect is driven by individual psychology (present bias, cognitive cost), not by trust in an employer as intermediary — exactly the evidence needed to judge whether the employer-plan default literature's mechanism transfers to a self-directed consumer banking app.
limitations: salary-linked savings account tied to an employer, not a fully independent consumer app
Afghan labor-market context differs from an EU digital banking population
does not directly test anchoring on preset contribution levels
relevance_reason: Uniquely isolates the psychological mechanism of default effects (rather than employer trust), which the brief flags as the key uncertainty in transferring pension-default evidence to a consumer app.

key_finding: A field experiment with payment reminders in a consumer credit card/checking platform in Brazil reduced late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil; heterogeneity analysis by prior overdraft history.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's worry made concrete with numbers: a well-intentioned behavioural nudge in a consumer, self-directed fintech setting can help most users but net-harm a vulnerable subgroup, which is exactly the distributional risk the round-up default decision needs to be checked against before shipping opt-out.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchors, so C1/C3/C6 are not addressed
